960.title: The flute and the song offerings
960.hook: a small reed flute, carried over hills, played by someone else's breath
960.carry: bhakti: we offer god what god gave first
960.tomorrow: God in the dust of the road
960.howItsDone: Many Hindus offer food to God at a home shrine or temple and receive it back as prasad; Tagore's Gitanjali songs, first written in Bengali, are still sung at home, in schools and at gatherings in Bengal.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Gandhi's Gita with the person of steady wisdom: the tortoise drawing in, the sea staying level while the rivers pour in.

A reed flute is a plain thing. A hollow stalk, a few holes, nothing inside. It makes no sound on its own; somebody has to breathe through it. In 1912, a Bengali poet came to London with English versions of his own songs. The Irish poet W. B. Yeats read them, wrote the introduction, and the book came out that year with the subtitle Song Offerings. The next year its author became the first writer from outside Europe to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. The poet is Rabindranath Tagore. The book is Gitanjali, and its first poem is about that flute.
screen: `A REED FLUTE MAKES NO SOUND ALONE.` → `1912: SONG OFFERINGS.` → `TAGORE'S GITANJALI.`

segments.voice: Here is how the first poem opens, in Tagore's own English: "Thou hast made me endless, such is thy pleasure. This frail vessel thou emptiest again and again, and fillest it ever with fresh life." Then the flute: this little reed has been carried over hills and dales, and thou has breathed through it melodies always new. The singer doesn't make the music. He's the instrument. That flips the title around. A song offering sounds like a gift a person makes and hands up to God. Here the songs were breathed in from the other side first, and what's offered back was given. That is the heart of bhakti, loving devotion. In the Gita, Krishna says: offer me a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water, with love, and I accept it. The leaf and the fruit were never ours to begin with. At home shrines and in temples, families offer food to God, then take it back as prasad: the same food, now a gift returned. Tagore's poem ends on hands: the infinite gifts come only on these very small hands, ages pass, and still thou pourest, and still there is room to fill. He never names a god here; some readers hear Krishna, always pictured with a flute. Either way the bhakti question for a gift you give today, a meal, a song, a day's work, isn't how much did I make. It's what was I given, that I'm handing back.
screen: `EMPTIED AND FILLED AGAIN.` · `THE SINGER IS THE FLUTE.` · `A LEAF, A FLOWER, A FRUIT, WATER.` · `PRASAD: THE GIFT COMES BACK.` · then, large: `WE OFFER WHAT WAS GIVEN.`

segments.voice: Let your hands rest open in your lap, palms up: small hands. Breathe out fully, then let the next breath come in on its own, and notice that you didn't make it; it arrived. Now bring to mind one thing you'll give today, a meal, a song, a piece of work. If you pray, offer it in your own words to the one you pray to, as a gift returned; if not, just notice what in it was given to you first.
Tagore's Gitanjali. Song offerings from a poet who pictures himself as a flute: what he gives back to God was breathed into him first.

961.title: God in the dust of the road
961.hook: a poet tells a worshiper to open the temple doors and look outside
961.carry: seva: god is with the ones who work
961.howItsDone: Many Hindu temples run kitchens where volunteers cook and serve whoever comes, and many families count this seva as worship alongside prayer with beads, flowers and incense.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tagore's Gitanjali opened with a reed flute: bhakti, where we offer God what God gave first.

A dark corner of a temple. The doors are shut. Someone sits there with a string of beads, chanting, eyes closed. It's a real and honored form of devotion. And in one Gitanjali poem, the poet walks up to that person and says, in effect: stop. Open your eyes. Your God isn't before you. Today, poem eleven, and where Tagore says to look instead.
screen: `A DARK CORNER, DOORS SHUT.` → `OPEN YOUR EYES.` → `WHERE TO LOOK INSTEAD.`

segments.voice: Here are the opening lines, in Tagore's own English: "Leave this chanting and singing and telling of beads! Whom dost thou worship in this lonely dark corner of a temple with doors all shut? Open thine eyes and see thy God is not before thee!" Then he says where God is: "He is there where the tiller is tilling the hard ground and where the pathmaker is breaking stones." God is with them in sun and in shower, the poem says, his garment covered in dust, and it tells the worshiper to put off the holy mantle and come down onto the dusty soil too. Tagore's family belonged to the Brahmo Samaj, a reform movement wary of image worship, and the poem carries that voice. Hindus who pray with beads and flowers may answer that their worship is where they learn to see God in the field. But both stand on one old teaching. In the Gita, Krishna says the Lord dwells in the heart of every being. If that's true, God isn't only behind the shut doors. The poem even asks where deliverance could be found, since the master himself has joyfully taken on the bonds of creation. Hindus have a word for worship done with the hands: seva, service. Temple kitchens run on it, volunteers chopping and stirring so anyone who walks in can eat, and many families count that hour as worship, not time away from it. The poem closes: meet him and stand by him in toil and in the sweat of thy brow. The place of worship and the place of work turn out to be the same place.

If you pray, you can hold that person in your prayer, right where they're working; if not, simply keep them in view, with some gratitude.

962.title: A mind without fear
962.hook: a sage tells a king he has reached fearlessness, and a poet asks the same for a whole people
962.carry: abhaya: the raised palm says fear not
962.tomorrow: Arjuna asks, why act at all?
962.howItsDone: Many Hindu images show the abhaya mudra, the raised open palm that means fear not; Tagore's 'Where the mind is without fear' is a poem some readers learn by heart and recite at school or at gatherings about freedom.

screen: `TAGORE'S GITANJALI.` · `SEVA: GOD WITH THE ONES WHO WORK.`

segments.voice: A king sits with a sage. The king is Janaka, ruler of Videha. The sage is Yajnavalkya. In the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad, Yajnavalkya asks the king where he'll go when he leaves this body, and the king admits he doesn't know. So the sage teaches him the Self: not this, not that, never grasped, never harmed. And at the end he says: Janaka, you have reached fearlessness. The king's answer is to wish the same gift back on his teacher, and to place his kingdom at the sage's service.
screen: `KING JANAKA AND THE SAGE.` → `THE SELF CAN'T BE HARMED.` → `JANAKA, YOU HAVE REACHED FEARLESSNESS.`

segments.voice: That word is abhaya, fearlessness, and it runs all through Hindu teaching. Another Upanishad, the Taittiriya, says that one who knows the bliss of Brahman fears nothing at all. Teachers often explain it this way: fear grips the small self that thinks it can be lost; knowing the deeper Self, which can't be harmed, loosens the grip. You can see the teaching in almost any temple. Look at the raised right hand on an image of Ganesha, or Lakshmi, or the dancing Shiva: palm open, fingers up, facing you. That's the abhaya mudra, the gesture that means fear not. Now Tagore. In one Gitanjali poem he stacks one small word, where, line on line: "Where the mind is without fear and the head is held high; Where knowledge is free; Where the world has not been broken up into fragments by narrow domestic walls." Then it lands as a prayer: "Into that heaven of freedom, my Father, let my country awake." Readers hear it about a nation waking, or about one person. Either way, it asks God for the gift Yajnavalkya named: a mind without fear. And here's where it meets your week. Before a test, a hard talk, a first day, the Hindu answer isn't just be brave. Many teachers put it this way: the deepest you, the Self, is not the thing at risk.
screen: `ABHAYA: FEARLESSNESS.` · `THE RAISED PALM: FEAR NOT.` · `WHERE THE MIND IS WITHOUT FEAR.` · `MY FATHER, LET MY COUNTRY AWAKE.` · then, large: `FEAR NOT.`

segments.voice: This is darshan, the Hindu practice of seeing God and being seen. Find an image with a raised palm, Ganesha, Lakshmi, the dancing Shiva, on a family altar, a phone, or in your mind. Sit with the head held high, chin level, neck long, without strain. Look at the open palm facing you. Name one fear sitting in you today, a test, a hard conversation, a phone call, and hear the gesture answer it: fear not. If you pray, end with Tagore's own line, into that heaven of freedom, my Father, let my country awake; if you don't, rest your eyes on the palm and notice what in you is still steady.

963.title: Arjuna asks, why act at all?
963.hook: Arjuna catches his teacher in what looks like a contradiction
963.carry: karma yoga: work offered to god doesn't bind
963.howItsDone: Some Hindus begin a day's work, or a meal, by mentally offering it to God, and some Gita study groups read chapter three alongside a classical commentary such as Shankara's.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed Tagore's Gitanjali with a prayer for a mind without fear: abhaya, the raised palm that says fear not.

If understanding is better than action, why push me into this terrible deed? That, in paraphrase, is how chapter three of the Gita begins. In chapter two, Krishna praised a steady understanding and said plain action falls far below it. And all along, he'd been telling Arjuna to stand up and fight. Arjuna is confused, and a little irritated. Your words seem mixed, he says. Tell me the one thing that's good for me. Now we read these chapters again, slowly, with the old commentators at our elbow.
screen: `WHY PUSH ME INTO THIS DEED?` → `YOUR WORDS SEEM MIXED.` → `READ AGAIN, WITH COMMENTARY.`

segments.voice: Nobody can stay even a moment without acting. Every being is made to act by the forces of its own nature. Sitting still is an act. Breathing is an act. So the question was never whether to act, but how. Here Krishna brings in an old word: yajna, sacrifice, offering. The world is bound by action, he says, except action done as offering. Do your work in that spirit, free of clinging. Then a short creation story. In the beginning, the Creator brought forth beings together with sacrifice and said: by this you will flourish. You nourish the gods, and the gods will nourish you. Rain, food, work, offering, rain again. Krishna calls it a wheel set turning, and says a person who takes from it and doesn't help turn it lives in vain. So karma, in chapter three, is first the plain word for action, and only then the web of consequences it sets going. This is karma yoga, the yoga of action: you can't stop working, so offer the work, and it stops binding you. It's why many Hindus offer food to God before they eat, or quietly offer a day's work before they begin it. Shankara, glossing sacrifice in this verse, says it means the Lord himself, and quotes an older Vedic line: sacrifice is Vishnu. So for him, action done as offering is action done for God. Either way, the verse says the same thing about the doer: act, and let go of the grip.
screen: `NOBODY STAYS A MOMENT WITHOUT ACTING.` · `THE QUESTION IS WHAT KIND OF ACTION.` · `ACTION DONE AS OFFERING DOESN'T BIND.` · `THE WHEEL: NOURISH AND BE NOURISHED.` · then, large: `KARMA YOGA: OFFER THE WORK.`

segments.voice: For the first few breaths, try to do nothing at all, and notice that you can't: the breath goes on, the heart goes on, the body keeps its balance. Then find one place in an ordinary day where you mostly take from the wheel and give little back, without judging it, and one small way to put something back. If you pray, you can hold that small return before Krishna, or the one you pray to.
Karma. In chapter three, first the plain word for action, which nobody escapes; done as an offering, it becomes karma yoga, and doesn't bind.

964.title: Why Krishna keeps working
964.hook: a king who reached the highest goal without leaving the palace
964.carry: lokasangraha: act to hold the world together
964.tomorrow: Taught to the sun, told again
964.howItsDone: Some Hindus who study the Gita point to King Janaka as the model of a person who lives in the world and knows the Self, and some study circles dwell on the verse on one's own dharma (3.35).

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma yoga in chapter three: nobody stays a moment without acting, and work offered to God doesn't bind.

Janaka was a king. He had a palace, a court, a kingdom to run: taxes, quarrels, harvests. Two days ago we watched the sage Yajnavalkya tell him he'd reached fearlessness, and the Hindu tradition remembers him that way, a sage who knew the Self while sitting on a throne. Halfway through chapter three, Krishna reaches for his name. Janaka and others like him, he says, reached perfection through action itself. Not by walking away. By doing the work. Then Krishna names someone else who never stops working: himself.
screen: `JANAKA: A KING AND A SAGE.` → `PERFECTION THROUGH ACTION.` → `KRISHNA KEEPS WORKING TOO.`

segments.voice: The word is lokasangraha. Loka is the world, the people in it. Sangraha is a holding together, a gathering. Krishna tells Arjuna to act with that in view. Then he gives a very human reason. Whatever a leading person does, others do too. Whatever standard they set, the world follows. So the way you work isn't private. Somebody is watching. Then Krishna points at himself. There's nothing in the three worlds, he says, that I have to do, nothing I lack, nothing to gain. And yet I keep acting. If I stopped, people everywhere would follow my path, and the worlds would fall apart. So the wise should act without attachment, as the unwise act with it, for the sake of holding the world together. And they shouldn't unsettle the minds of people attached to their work; let them keep working, and show them how by example. A few verses later: better one's own dharma, even done imperfectly, than another's done well. Your own place in the holding-together, even if it's clumsy. Commentators weigh this differently. Shankara, who holds that liberation finally comes through knowledge, reads the call to act here as fitting for those still on the way, and as an example for others. Some modern readers took lokasangraha as close to the heart of the whole Gita. Bal Gangadhar Tilak, in his long commentary called the Gita Rahasya, read it that way, as a charge to keep working for the world's welfare. The verses can carry both. Either way, karma here isn't only my action. It's one thread in a cloth that a lot of other people are wearing.

965.title: Taught to the sun, told again
965.hook: the sun, a king, his son, and a teaching handed down until it was lost
965.carry: whenever dharma declines, god comes again
965.howItsDone: In Hindu teaching lineages, a teaching is received from a teacher in an unbroken parampara, and Gita 4.7–8, 'whenever dharma declines', is a verse some Hindus learn by heart.

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma as lokasangraha: King Janaka reaching perfection through action, and Krishna working to lokasangraha: act to hold the world together.
screen: `KARMA.` · `LOKASANGRAHA: ACT TO HOLD THE WORLD TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: The sun. Manu. Ikshvaku. Three names at the start of chapter four, and they're a chain. Krishna says he taught this yoga, the yoga of action, to Vivasvan, the sun. Vivasvan told it to Manu. Manu told it to his son Ikshvaku. And so it was handed on, from one royal sage to the next. Then, over a long stretch of time, Krishna says, it was lost. That's why he's telling it again, now, to Arjuna, on a battlefield.
screen: `THE SUN, MANU, IKSHVAKU.` → `HANDED ON, KING TO KING.` → `LOST, AND TOLD AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The Gita's word for this handing on is parampara: one after another, teacher to student. And Krishna tells Arjuna why it's coming to him: because you are my devotee and my friend, and this is a deep secret. Arjuna, being Arjuna, hears a problem. Your birth was recent, he says. The sun's was long ago. How could you have taught him? Krishna's answer is the turn of the chapter. Many births have passed, for me and for you. I know them all. You don't. Then he describes his own coming. Though unborn, and Lord of all beings, he comes into being through his own power, his own maya. And he says when: whenever dharma declines and its opposite rises, he sends himself forth, age after age, to protect the good and set dharma back on its feet. This is the teaching behind every avatar story Hindus tell, Rama, Krishna, the fish, the man-lion. The word avatara, a coming down, isn't in these verses, but these are the verses people quote for it. And here's the link to our word. In the next verse, Krishna calls his birth and his action, his karma, divine. Whoever truly knows them isn't born again on leaving the body, but comes to him. So the one teaching the yoga of action is also acting: taking birth, entering the world, doing the work. The commentators read his coming differently. Shankara speaks of the Lord appearing to take a body by his own maya, while remaining unborn. Ramanuja insists the Lord's births are real, taken freely by his own will, not forced on him by karma, as ours are.
screen: `PARAMPARA: ONE AFTER ANOTHER.` · `MANY BIRTHS: I KNOW THEM, YOU DON'T.` · `AVATARA: THE COMING DOWN.` · `HIS BIRTH AND KARMA ARE DIVINE.` · then, large: `WHENEVER DHARMA DECLINES, I COME.`

966.hook: a verse said over a plate of food, where everything in the meal is Brahman

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma handed down: whenever dharma declines, god comes again, and the promise that whenever dharma declines, God comes again.

Before the first bite, in some Hindu homes, someone says a line in Sanskrit over the plate. Brahmarpanam brahma havir. It's from chapter four of the Gita, an odd thing to say before dinner: it's a verse about a fire sacrifice. The offering is Brahman. The thing offered is Brahman. It's poured into the fire, which is Brahman, by the one offering, who is Brahman. A meal, a fire, a giver, all one.
screen: `A LINE SAID OVER THE PLATE.` → `THE OFFERING IS BRAHMAN.` → `ONE ACT, SEEN ALL THE WAY THROUGH.`

segments.voice: A few verses earlier, Krishna sets a puzzle. What is action, and what is inaction? Even the wise are confused about this. His answer: the one who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, is wise among people, and does all their work in yoga. Shankara reads this as seeing that the Self never acts, even while the body is busy. Ramanuja reads it as seeing knowledge of the self alive inside work done without attachment. Then Krishna describes such a person. Their acts have been burned in the fire of knowledge. They've let go of clinging to the fruit; they're always content, depending on nothing, and though they keep acting, they do nothing at all. Then the meal verse: Brahman is the offering, Brahman the oblation, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman. The one who sees Brahman in the act goes to Brahman. Our word has traveled since chapter three began: action you can't avoid, done as offering; action for the world, the way Janaka did it; action handed down through teachers and taken up by God; and now action seen so clearly that the doer, the deed and the fire are one thing. Later in the chapter Krishna says it plainly: as a kindled fire turns wood to ash, the fire of knowledge turns all actions to ash. Look back over the week: Tagore's flute, God in the dust, a mind without fear. And the Gita's long answer to Arjuna's complaint: you can't stop acting, so learn to see what acting is.
screen: `INACTION IN ACTION, ACTION IN INACTION.` · `ACTS BURNED IN THE FIRE OF KNOWLEDGE.` · `BRAHMAN OFFERS BRAHMAN INTO BRAHMAN.` · `THE WEEK: FLUTE, DUST, FEARLESSNESS, WHEEL, FIRE.` · then, large: `SEE THE ACT ALL THE WAY THROUGH.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the last thing you ate, or the next, and go through it the way the verse does: the food, the hands that lift it, the hunger it goes into, the one who's eating, each part slowly, then all of them together as one act. If you pray, you can say the verse's opening words, brahmarpanam brahma havir, or a grace from your own tradition; if not, simply rest in the whole act at once.
